750.title: Benedict in the cave (c. 500)
750.hook: a student leaves Rome in disgust and lives three years in a cave at Subiaco
750.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Benedict as a saint and a founder of monastic life, and pilgrims visit the Sacred Cave at Subiaco, where a monastery now stands around the place he lived.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo's Christmas sermon: Christian, recognize your dignity. Your line was know your dignity.

A rope comes down a rock face, with a loaf of bread tied to the end and a little bell on it. Below, in a cave in the hills east of Rome, a young man hears the bell, reaches out, and takes his bread. Up above, a monk named Romanus has saved it from his own meals. He does this day after day, for a young man nobody else knows is there. The young man is Benedict. He was supposed to be a student in Rome.
screen: `A ROPE, A LOAF, A BELL.` → `A MONK ABOVE.` → `A YOUNG MAN BELOW.`

segments.voice: Our source is Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote Benedict's life in his Dialogues and says he heard it from Benedict's own disciples. Benedict came from a good family in the region of Nursia, and was sent to Rome to study. There he looked around. Gregory says he saw many of the students sliding into vice, and pulled back the foot he'd just set in the world, afraid that if he took in too much of it, he'd fall in headlong himself. So he left his books, his father's house and his inheritance, wanting to please God alone. Gregory has a phrase worth keeping: Benedict left knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned. He wasn't running from learning. He was running from a kind of life. Next, the cave. Benedict went to a wild place called Subiaco. On the way he met Romanus, a monk, who gave him the monk's habit and kept his secret. Benedict lived in a narrow cave, Gregory says, for three years, unknown to everyone except Romanus, who lowered bread to him on that rope with its bell. Gregory adds that the devil once threw a stone and broke the bell. Romanus kept feeding him anyway. And here's the twist. Eventually shepherds found him, and at first took him for a wild animal, dressed as he was in skins. But once they talked with him, many of them changed their lives. The hiding place started to become a gathering place. Catholics still visit the cave at Subiaco today, with a monastery built around it.
screen: `A STUDENT IN ROME.` · `KNOWINGLY IGNORANT.` · `THREE YEARS IN A CAVE.` · `THE SHEPHERDS FIND HIM.` · then, large: `AWAY FROM ROME.`

segments.voice: Step away from one noisy thing, the phone in your hand, a room with a television, a group chat that never stops: put the phone face down or in another room, and find a corner, a chair, a car parked somewhere quiet. Let that be your cave, and listen to what's left when the noise is gone. If you pray, use the time the way Benedict did, simply to be with God.

Your line: away from rome. A little quiet goes a long way. Seven hundred fifty days now.

751.title: Monte Cassino
751.hook: Benedict founds his monastery and writes a Rule for beginners
751.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying the psalms together at set hours, working and reading, and some communities read a passage of the Rule aloud each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict in the specus at Subiaco, fed with bread on a rope. Your line was away from rome.

Listen. That's the first word. Not pray, not obey, not work. Listen, my son, to the teachings of the master, and bend the ear of your heart. That's how Benedict opens the short book monks and nuns would live by long after him. He wrote it on a mountain called Monte Cassino, where he'd come with his monks after years of building small communities around Subiaco.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.` → `THE EAR OF YOUR HEART.` → `A BOOK ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Gregory the Great tells how Benedict came to Cassino. On the height stood an old temple to Apollo, where country people still offered sacrifice. Benedict broke the idol, built two chapels in its place, one to Saint Martin and one to Saint John the Baptist, and preached to the people around, calling them to faith. A mountain of old worship became a mountain of prayer. Next, the Rule. Gregory says Benedict wrote a rule for monks, outstanding for its discretion and clear in its language, and that anyone who wanted to know how Benedict lived could find it there, because he couldn't have taught otherwise than he lived. What's in it? A day built from prayer, work and reading. Monks gather to sing the psalms at set hours, day and night. They work with their hands. They read. They eat together and listen to reading at meals. The abbot is told to remember he'll answer to God for every one of them, and to adjust to the weak as well as the strong. The Rule even tells the abbot to call everyone to counsel, because God often reveals what is better to the younger. Now the line that gives us today's carry. In the last chapter, Benedict calls his own work a little rule for beginners. Not a masterpiece: a beginning, written so people could start. He points beyond it to the scriptures and the Fathers for anyone who wants to go higher. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by it today, and on Monte Cassino, monks still pray.
screen: `A TEMPLE BECOMES CHAPELS.` · `A RULE CLEAR AND WISE.` · `PRAYER, WORK, READING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.`

If you pray, ask to hear God, and that person, with the ear of your heart.

752.title: Monks as keepers
752.hook: as Rome fell, monasteries copied and kept books
752.howItsDone: Catholic monasteries kept libraries and copied books by hand, and Benedictine communities still set aside daily hours for sacred reading, called lectio divina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monte Cassino, where Benedict wrote what he called a little rule for beginners. Your line was a little rule for beginners.

How does a book outlast the world that made it? One answer sits at a sloping desk, with a quill, a pot of ink, and a sheet of animal skin scraped smooth. A monk bends over it, copying one letter at a time from an older book propped beside him. His back aches. His fingers are stained. The light from the window is fading. Outside the walls, the old Roman world is coming apart. Inside, he finishes a line, checks it against the original, and dips the pen again.
screen: `A QUILL AND A SKIN.` → `ONE LETTER AT A TIME.` → `OUTSIDE, A WORLD UNRAVELS.`

segments.voice: A scriptorium is a monastery's writing room, where monks copied books by hand. Why did monks need books at all? Benedict's Rule, which we met yesterday, sets aside hours every day for reading. And in Lent, it says, each monk is to receive a book from the library and read it straight through. So a monastery needed a library, and a library needs copies. Next, a man who praised copying as holy work. Cassiodorus founded a monastery called Vivarium. In his book of instructions for its monks, he praises the copyist above almost any other kind of manual labor. The copyist, he says, preaches to people with his hand, and spreads the Lord's words to faraway places without leaving his seat. Every word copied, he says, is a wound to the devil. Now, what they kept. Scripture first: the Gospels, the Psalms, the whole Bible. Then the Fathers: Augustine, Jerome, the ones we've been meeting these past weeks. And alongside them, some readers point out, the monks also copied grammar books and works of pagan authors, because you needed good Latin to read scripture well. The world outside could be loud and violent and falling apart, and inside, someone was sitting at a desk, making sure the next generation would have something to read. Not by fighting. By sitting still and copying, line after line, in a room set apart for it. When you open a Bible today, part of its long road ran through rooms like that one.

segments.voice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper, and choose one line worth keeping: a verse, a line from a prayer you know, a sentence someone once said to you that stayed. Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk at the desk did, then read it once, quietly, and check it against where it came from. If you pray, let the line you copied become your prayer.

753.title: Columba of Iona (563)
753.hook: an Irish monk exiles himself to an island and sends missions to Scotland
753.howItsDone: Catholics in Ireland and Scotland keep the feast of Saint Columba, also called Colmcille, and pilgrims still travel to Iona.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scriptorium, the monks' copying room. Your line was they kept the books.

A white horse, the one that carries the milk pails, walks up to a tired man resting by the road on a small island. It lays its head on his chest and, in the story, begins to weep. His servant moves to drive it away. The old man stops him. Let it be, he says; it loves me, and it knows I'm leaving. That man is Columba, an Irish monk, and the island is Iona, off the coast of what's now Scotland. He came there by choice, and it was there he died.
screen: `A WHITE HORSE WEEPS.` → `IT KNOWS HE'S LEAVING.` → `AN IRISH MONK ON IONA.`

segments.voice: Our source is Adomnán, a later abbot of Iona, who wrote Columba's life from what the community remembered. He gives Columba's reason for leaving Ireland in a single phrase: he sailed away wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ. Not someone who goes to a holy place and comes back, but someone who leaves home for good, for God's sake, and lives as a stranger. A later story says he left as a penance, after a quarrel that ended in a battle; Adomnán gives no such reason. On Iona, Columba built a monastery. Monks prayed, farmed, fished, studied, and copied scripture, and Adomnán shows Columba himself at a writing desk. From that small island, monks went out. Adomnán tells of Columba traveling to the fortress of Bridei, a king of the Picts. The king shut his gates against him. Columba made the sign of the cross on the doors, knocked, and, in Adomnán's telling, the bolts drew back on their own, and the king came out to meet him with respect. Now the end. In his last days, Adomnán says, Columba was copying the psalms in his hut. He reached a verse saying that those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing, and stopped there. Let the next part be written by the one who comes after me, he said, meaning his successor. That night he went to the church for the midnight prayer and died before the altar, surrounded by his monks. Catholics honor him as a saint, and Iona is still a place of pilgrimage. An island at the edge of the map became, for a time, a center that sent people out.
screen: `A PILGRIM FOR CHRIST.` · `A MONASTERY ON IONA.` · `THE GATES OF THE PICTISH KING.` · `HE STOPS AT A PSALM.` · then, large: `THE ISLAND.`

754.title: Gregory the Great (540–604)
754.hook: he calls himself servant of the servants of God
754.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Pope Saint Gregory the Great, and popes still use the title servant of the servants of God in solemn documents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columba of Iona, a peregrinus, the pilgrim for Christ who built a monastery at the edge of the map. Your line was the island.

Servant of the servants of God. That's what one bishop of Rome called himself in his letters. He was a monk who didn't want the job. His name was Gregory. He came from a wealthy Roman family, gave his life to prayer, and founded a monastery in the city itself. He's the same Gregory who wrote down Benedict's life. Then Rome's bishop died, and the people of Rome chose Gregory.
screen: `SERVANT OF SERVANTS.` → `A MONK WHO DIDN'T WANT IT.` → `ROME CHOOSES GREGORY.`

segments.voice: Pope is what Catholics call the bishop of Rome, whom they understand as the successor of Saint Peter and the shepherd of the whole Church. Start with Gregory's reluctance. Gregory of Tours, in his History of the Franks, says Gregory tried to escape it, even writing to the emperor asking him not to approve the choice. It didn't work; he was made bishop of Rome anyway. Next, what he did with it. Rome was battered by flood and plague. Gregory of Tours describes him calling the whole city out to pray, walking in processions through the streets while the sickness went on. He kept writing letters, which still survive, to bishops, rulers and ordinary people. He also wrote a book on how a pastor should live, calling the care of souls the art of arts. Now the title. When the bishop of Constantinople used the title universal bishop, Gregory objected in his letters: that title, he said, was too proud for any bishop. For himself, he kept using another: servant of the servants of God. It echoes something Jesus tells his disciples in the Gospels: whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all. Gregory took that teaching and made it his name. Catholics believe the pope has real authority. Gregory's point is about how it's held. A servant of servants is at the bottom of the ladder, serving the very people who serve. In Gregory's hands, the office Catholics see as the highest in the Church described itself from the lowest place. Catholics call him Saint Gregory the Great, pope and Doctor of the Church.
screen: `THE BISHOP OF ROME.` · `HE TRIED TO ESCAPE IT.` · `PLAGUE, PRAYER, THE ART OF ARTS.` · `A TITLE FROM THE LOWEST PLACE.` · then, large: `SERVANT OF SERVANTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who serve you without much notice, the driver of your bus, the person who cleans your office, a cashier, a nurse, a parent who cooks, and pick one. 755.title: Not Angles but angels
755.hook: the story goes Gregory saw English boys in a market, and later sent Augustine of Canterbury (597)
755.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Augustine of Canterbury as the apostle of the English and Saint Gregory the Great as the pope who sent him, and both have feasts on the Church's calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory the Great, the pope who called himself servant of servants. Your line was servant of servants.

A market in Rome. Merchants have arrived with goods to sell, and among the goods, the story says, are boys: fair-skinned, light-haired, good-looking. A Roman monk stops and stares. He asks where they're from. Britain, he's told. Are they Christians? No. He sighs, and asks the name of their people. Angles, they tell him. And the monk, who is Gregory, before he became pope, says something people have retold ever since.
screen: `A MARKET IN ROME.` → `BOYS FROM BRITAIN.` → `THEY ARE CALLED ANGLES.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Bede, an English monk who wrote a history of the Church among his own people. He's careful to say it was handed down from those before him. In Bede's telling, Gregory answers: good, for they have the faces of angels, and such people ought to share heaven with the angels. The neat phrase, not Angles but angels, is how later people shortened it. Bede has Gregory keep going. Their region is called Deira; Gregory turns that into the Latin for from wrath: they'll be rescued from wrath. Their king is Ælle. Then, says Gregory, Alleluia must be sung there. Three puns in a row. Next, what he did. Bede says Gregory asked to go to Britain himself, but the people of Rome wouldn't let him leave. Later, as pope, he sent others: a monk named Augustine and a band of monks. Not the Augustine of the Confessions; this is Augustine of Canterbury. Now the wobble. Bede says that partway there, the monks lost their nerve. They'd heard the people were fierce, and they didn't know the language. They sent Augustine back to ask Gregory to call it off. Gregory wrote back and told them to go on. And the landing. Bede says they came to the king of Kent, whose wife was already a Christian. The king met them outdoors, worried about magic indoors. They came carrying a silver cross and a picture of Christ painted on a board, singing as they walked. The king let them stay and preach, and gave them a place in Canterbury. That's the mission to the English: a pun in a market, and a group of frightened monks who kept going.
screen: `BEDE'S HANDED-DOWN STORY.` · `ANGELS, WRATH, ALLELUIA.` · `THE MONKS LOSE THEIR NERVE.` · `A SILVER CROSS IN KENT.` · then, large: `THE MISSION TO THE ENGLISH.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine: Gregory's pun in a market, and the monks he sent who wanted to turn back. Your line was the mission to the english.

No drums. No chords. No beat to tap your foot to. A single line of melody rises, hangs on one syllable for a long, winding moment, and settles again. A handful of voices or a whole choir, all singing the same notes at the same time, so it sounds almost like one person breathing. The words are Latin, often from the psalms or other scripture. It can be heard in monasteries before dawn, in cathedrals on feast days, in a small parish choir on a Sunday. It's called Gregorian chant, and it carries a pope's name.
screen: `NO DRUMS, NO CHORDS.` → `ONE LINE OF MELODY.` → `MANY VOICES, ONE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Gregorian chant is the Church's own sung prayer: the psalms and texts of the Mass and the hours, set to a single melody sung in unison. Start with the name. Tradition links this music to Pope Gregory, the same Gregory we've been with these past days, and medieval pictures sometimes show him with a dove at his ear, as if the Holy Spirit were singing to him. Some readers think the chant as we have it took shape after his time, and that his name was given to honor him. Either way, the name stuck. Next, the shape. In unison means everyone sings the same note at once. Nobody takes the harmony or the solo. Your voice disappears into the others, and the words float on top. Then, why it's built that way. Benedict's Rule tells monks to stand and sing the psalms so that their mind agrees with their voice. Chant is made for that. It goes at the speed of the words, with no beat to march to, so you follow the text and the breath. And Saint Paul tells the early Christians to speak to one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in their hearts to the Lord. Now, the Church today. The Second Vatican Council says the Church recognizes Gregorian chant as especially suited to the Roman liturgy, and that it should have a first place in worship, other things being equal. Here, after a week of monks and a pope, is a way of singing the psalms: one voice made of many.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S SUNG PRAYER.` · `NAMED FOR GREGORY.` · `EVERYONE ON ONE NOTE.` · `MIND IN TUNE WITH VOICE.` · then, large: `ONE VOICE.`

segments.voice: If you can, play some chant and let it run; if not, remember the sound from the start of this lesson, one line rising and falling, many voices on the same note. Either way, don't follow the Latin; follow the breath, and let your breathing slow to the pace of a long syllable. If you pray, let the chant carry your prayer without words.
